tone_statements.citation: Blench, Roger M. 2026. Phonology of the TuGbiri Language [grh] of Central Nigeria. Circulation draft (printout dated 9 February 2026), 13 pp. Cambridge: Kay Williamson Educational Foundation (KWEF). Posted on Academia.edu (item 144927734, online since Nov 2025).
tone_statements.quote: Tugbiri has two underlying level tones, a falling tone and a rare rising tone. It has abundant downstep and rarer upstep and thus sounds as if it has three phonetic tones. In rare cases, double downstep results in four phonetic tone levels. The question morpheme ǎ has rising tone, but this is exceptional. [...] Contour tones are almost completely absent and around 80% of all verbs have the tonal profile L(L)H, while many of the remainder have the profile HH.

sources.note: Table of languages (p.48): 'Western — Gbiri — Vigorous — Wenger (2016)'; 'Niragu — Vigorous — Wenger (2016)'; acknowledgement p.47 'Thanks to Rachelle Wenger for information on Gbiri'; Table 12 'arm, hand': Gbiri ka-kyara pl. na-, Niragu ka-tʃara (BCCW 'Kahu'). sources.citation: Blench, Roger M. 2018. Nominal affixing in the Kainji languages of northwestern and central Nigeria. In John R. Watters (ed.), East Benue-Congo: Nouns, pronouns, and verbs (Niger-Congo Comparative Studies 1), 59–106. Berlin: Language Science Press.

sources.citation: Blench, Roger. 2004 (ms). The status of the East Kainji languages of Central Nigeria: recent research. Paper for the Hamburg meeting (Gerhardt retirement), 2 Oct 2004. 12 pp.
sources.note: Section 3.1 'Phonology' and 'Tones' describe eBoze (four level tones plus glides) and tiMap; Gbiri and Niragu are named only in the history (Meek 1931 wordlists), Appendix 1 list and Appendix 3 ('arm, hand': Gbiri *u-kula, Niragu ka-tSara). Nothing on Gbiri-Niragu stress or tone.

sources.note: Section 3.3 Tones (p.9): two underlying level tones (H, L) plus a falling (HL) tone and a rare rising (LH) tone; abundant downstep and rarer upstep, so the language sounds as if it had three phonetic tones, and double downstep can give four phonetic levels in one word; downstep/upstep never on an initial syllable (analysed as step tones, written with a macron); unlike related Boze, no complex contour tones; minimal pairs for H vs L (pùrú 'sleep' / púrú 'grab'); c. 80% of verbs L(L)H, most others HH; long vs doubled vowels distinguished by a tone change (3.1.2); section 4: orthography does not…
